name: Machilipatnam (Pedana) block-printed Kalamkari
summary: Machilipatnam Kalamkari is a hand-block-printed cotton textile tradition from Pedana and neighbouring villages near Machilipatnam (Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh), registered as a Geographical Indication (application no. 90; certificate 2008). Cloth is bleached, treated with myrobalan, block-printed with iron (kasim) and alum (karam) mordants, boiled in alizarin with plant additives, overprinted with yellow and indigo, and fixed through repeated washing in flowing water and sun-drying. The tradition descends from the Golconda-era port trade in Masulipatnam painted and printed cottons for Persia and Europe, where blocks progressively replaced the hand-drawn kalam.

concepts.title: Machilipatnam (Pedana) block-printed Kalamkari
concepts.summary: Machilipatnam Kalamkari is a registered Geographical Indication (application no. 90) filed by the Vegetable Hand-block Kalamkari Printers Association, Pedana, for handicraft goods in classes 24, 25 and 27.
concepts.body_md:
Machilipatnam Kalamkari is a registered Geographical Indication (application no. 90) filed by the Vegetable Hand-block Kalamkari Printers Association, Pedana, for handicraft goods in classes 24, 25 and 27. [S1]

It is hand-block-printed fabric using vegetable dyes from Pedana, about 13 km from Machilipatnam, and is one of two kalamkari styles, the other being Srikalahasti. [S3]

Through this art form cotton fabrics are painted freehand or with blocks using vegetable dyes; the GI registration includes the dye recipes and stages of application. [S2]

The base cloth is printed and dyed with mordants (iron acetate, alum) and dyes such as alizarin, myrobalan and indigo. [S4]

The tradition is also referred to as Pedana kalamkari or the Machilipatnam style. [S16, S2]

concepts.title: Golconda patronage and the port of Masulipatnam
concepts.summary: The rulers at Golconda patronised kalamkari of Masulipatnam (now Machilipatnam) during the 16th and 17th centuries; textiles were made for the Sultanate and Persia/Iran and customised to Islamic taste.
concepts.body_md:
The rulers at Golconda patronised kalamkari of Masulipatnam (now Machilipatnam) during the 16th and 17th centuries; textiles were made for the Sultanate and Persia/Iran and customised to Islamic taste. [S6]

Kalamkari flourished at Masulipatnam; the craft began in the old city of Golconda and spread along the eastern coast. [S5]

The Machilipatnam style developed under Mughal rule and was practised under the Golconda Sultanate. [S3]

Machilipatnam was a busy port during the late medieval period, especially the 15th-17th centuries; its textiles were meant for clothes, prayer mats, bedspreads, tapestries and hangings. [S13]

concepts.title: Export to Persia/Iran
concepts.summary: An 1879 Machilipatnam dress fabric was probably made for export to Iran; its Persian inscription names the trader and calls the textile qalamkar, a printed imitation of hand-drawn kalamkari.

concepts.title: Coromandel chintz and the European trade
concepts.summary: Chintz was imported in large quantities into Britain and the Netherlands in the 17th and 18th centuries, and its mordant/resist techniques are particularly associated with the Coromandel Coast.
concepts.body_md:
Chintz was imported in large quantities into Britain and the Netherlands in the 17th and 18th centuries, and its mordant/resist techniques are particularly associated with the Coromandel Coast. [S11]

The textiles were originally known as Coromandel chintz and were traded in the 17th century mainly to Europe and Iran. [S5]

The English called it chintz, the Dutch sitz, the Portuguese pintado; Masulipatnam was the main centre for trade with the west. [S6]

concepts.title: Shift from pen (kalam) to block
concepts.summary: Kalams were replaced by blocks in the nineteenth century.
concepts.body_md:
Kalams were replaced by blocks in the nineteenth century. [S5]

Early chintz was drawn with a bamboo pen and patterned with mordants and resists; block printing later replaced much of this work. [S8]

In Masulipatnam hand-carved block prints were used with finer details done with the kalam; the shift from kalam to block happened as designs were repetitive. [S6]

The industry suffered until 1952, when the All India Handicrafts Board under Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay revived the craft. [S6]

concepts.title: Producer communities and karkhana organisation
concepts.summary: The main castes engaged are Devangas, Padmasalis, Kannebhaktulu and Senapathalu; dyers and printers belonged to Hindu or Muslim faiths; blocks were made by specialist block makers, sometimes by printers themselves.
concepts.body_md:
The main castes engaged are Devangas, Padmasalis, Kannebhaktulu and Senapathalu; dyers and printers belonged to Hindu or Muslim faiths; blocks were made by specialist block makers, sometimes by printers themselves. [S4]

Machilipatnam printing takes place in karkhanas where block making, washing and printing happen simultaneously, unlike family-based hand-painted kalamkari. [S3, S13]

Block makers are mostly from the carpenter community. [S13]

Block makers interviewed in Pedana say the printing technique was first introduced by the rangrez (dyers) community, and that very few people now make blocks in Andhra Pradesh. [S14]

concepts.title: Myrobalan (karakkaya)
concepts.summary: Myrobalan solution is prepared from karakkaya, pounded, boiled at least 2.5 hours, filtered, and kept overnight; the cloth dipped in it turns yellowish.
concepts.body_md:
Myrobalan solution is prepared from karakkaya, pounded, boiled at least 2.5 hours, filtered, and kept overnight; the cloth dipped in it turns yellowish. [S4]

The cloth is treated with myrobalan (karakayya) solution for 30–45 minutes, squeezed and dried in sunlight. [S3]

Myrobalan is identified as Terminalia chebula. [S6]

Yellow is applied with a brush using prepared myrobalan solution; boiling with myrobalan flowers alone gives yellow. [S4]

concepts.title: Kasim (iron acetate black mordant)
concepts.summary: Iron acetate (kasim in Telugu) is made from salt water, jaggery, iron strips and paddy husk; the strips are smouldered overnight, cleaned and fermented with jaggery-salt solution in a covered stone pot sunk 90% below ground.
concepts.body_md:
Iron acetate (kasim in Telugu) is made from salt water, jaggery, iron strips and paddy husk; the strips are smouldered overnight, cleaned and fermented with jaggery-salt solution in a covered stone pot sunk 90% below ground. [S4]

Black colour is made from iron scraps, jaggery and salt water sealed in a mud jar buried in soil for 21 days. [S15]

Small iron pieces are soaked in jaggery/starch/coconut water and left to ferment for a few days to make black. [S6]

Iron is used to produce black in Machilipatnam block printing. [S5]

concepts.title: Alum (karam)
concepts.summary: Alum (karam in Telugu) is pounded, boiled in water until reduced to half, and iron implements are avoided because iron darkens the colour.
concepts.body_md:
Alum (karam in Telugu) is pounded, boiled in water until reduced to half, and iron implements are avoided because iron darkens the colour. [S4]

Alum-based red paste is block-printed where red is needed, and different alum concentrations produce more shades. [S3]

Red is obtained using alum as mordant and then boiling the alum-printed fabric in alizarin. [S4, S5]

concepts.summary: Madder (Rubia) and chay (Oldenlandia umbellata) were highly estimated as fine sources of red in the south.

Alizarin is used today instead of organic matter. [S6]
